claims.text: The target component is a damaged nickel-based superalloy component, such as an Inconel 718 turbine part, exhibiting microcracking.
Conventional fusion-welding repair creates a hot-cracking risk for this nickel-based superalloy under high-temperature cyclic loading.
Friction stir repair can restore damaged high-value nickel-based superalloy components without melting the base material.
Customized or optimized tool geometries will enable effective friction stir repair of the damaged region.
Suitable proposed processing ranges are traverse speeds of 50–150 mm/min and rotational speeds of 600–1200 rpm.
Friction stirring produces severe plastic deformation in the repair region.
Severe plastic deformation during friction stirring induces dynamic recrystallization.
Dynamic recrystallization creates a fine-grained stir zone with a gradual transition to the base material.
Avoiding a liquid phase prevents hot-crack formation during repair.
Optimized tool geometry promotes uniform material flow and proper bonding at the repair interface.
Uniform material flow and proper interfacial bonding enhance fatigue resistance and high-temperature mechanical integrity.
The friction stir repaired region will have lower residual stress and lower crack-initiation propensity.
Friction stir repair will provide better fatigue life and mechanical performance under high-temperature cyclic loading than traditional fusion-weld repair.
Traditional fusion-welding repair involves melting that promotes hot cracking.
Traditional fusion-welding repair produces inferior interfacial microstructure and mechanical performance under aggressive cyclic thermal conditions.
The proposed repair can remain robust under cyclic loading at operating temperatures up to approximately 700°C.
The approach is limited to regions whose geometry permits effective tool engagement.
Extremely complex geometries or severe damage may prevent effective friction stir repair.
